chunks: And by this chain, from Sa'd ibn 'Abdillah, from Ahmad ibn Muhammad ibn 'Isa, from al-'Abbas ibn Ma'ruf, from Hammad ibn 'Isa, from Ibrahim ibn 'Amr al-Yamani, from Abu Khalid al-Qammat, that he heard Abu 'Abdillah (peace be upon him)
speaking about water that a man passes by, which is a stagnant pool containing a dead animal and carrion.

Abu 'Abdillah (peace be upon him) said: If the water's smell or taste has changed, do not drink from it and do not perform wudu from it. And if its smell and taste have not changed, drink and perform wudu.

key_terms.الْجِيفَةُ: putrid carcass; decomposing carrion, emphasizing advanced decay
key_terms.الْمَيْتَةُ: mayta; animal that died without proper Islamic slaughter, rendering it ritually impure
key_terms.تَغَيَّرَ: changed/altered; the decisive jurisprudential criterion for water impurity
key_terms.رِيحُهُ: its odor/smell; one of the two sensory criteria examined for water purity

ai.seo_question: What is Imam al-Sadiq's ruling on using stagnant water containing a dead animal for drinking and wudu?
ai.summary: Imam al-Sadiq (peace be upon him) establishes that stagnant water containing a dead animal or rotting carrion remains pure for drinking and wudu as long as its smell and taste are unaltered. The sensory criterion of taghyīr (alteration of smell or taste) is thus the operative jurisprudential marker distinguishing pure from impure water in Shia fiqh, situated here within the chapter on the quantity of water resistant to impurity.
